analysis.one_liner: Lets the Justice Department sue police departments over patterns of misconduct and makes police brutality a federal crime.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, never got a hearing or a vote and died with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for a government to run a police department in a way that repeatedly violates people's constitutional rights. The Attorney General or an injured person could sue in federal court to force change, and winning plaintiffs could recover attorney fees. It would also make excessive force by police a federal crime — punishable by up to life in prison if someone dies — and require police agencies to report excessive-force complaints to the Justice Department, with annual public summaries broken down by race.
analysis.who_benefits: People who suffer police misconduct would gain a direct federal lawsuit to stop department-wide patterns, with attorney fees covered, and a new federal criminal penalty for officers who use excessive force. Communities would gain public, nationwide data on excessive-force complaints, broken down by race, and states would have to report that data to keep receiving federal justice grants.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any government to engage in a pattern or practice of law-enforcement conduct that deprives people of constitutional or statutory rights, and lets the Attorney General sue for court-ordered relief to eliminate it.

Gives any injured person their own civil suit against such a pattern or practice, with reasonable attorney fees and litigation costs — including expert fees — available to a winning plaintiff, making such suits financially feasible.

Creates a federal crime of police brutality: an officer who uses more force than reasonably necessary faces a fine and up to life in prison if death results, up to 10 years for bodily injury, or up to one year otherwise.

Requires the Attorney General to collect and publish annual data on excessive-force complaints and to report to Congress on complaints against local police, broken down by the race of complainants and accused officers and by whether federal authorities investigated or prosecuted — with identities kept confidential and data used only for research.
Conditions state applications for federal justice-system improvement grants on certifying that state and local governments are providing excessive-force complaint data to the Attorney General.

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and other government bodies would bear the cost of federal pattern-or-practice lawsuits, attorney-fee awards when plaintiffs win, and new data-collection and reporting requirements. Officers who use excessive force would face new federal criminal exposure.

drawbacks.text: The criminal penalty would apply to force exceeding what is 'reasonably necessary' for a law-enforcement duty — a standard officers and their unions would argue is too vague and would second-guess split-second decisions, potentially up to life in prison.

The bill imposes data-collection and certification duties on state and local governments as a condition of federal grant money, adding administrative burden and giving the federal government leverage over local police agencies.
The remedies are limited to equitable and declaratory relief — courts ordering changes — rather than damages, so individual victims would still need separate suits to be compensated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap at the time: no federal cause of action targeted department-wide police misconduct, and no national data existed on excessive-force complaints. The main costs — litigation exposure for governments, a new criminal penalty with a flexible standard, and reporting burdens — fall on institutions rather than the public, though critics could fairly argue the criminal standard is broad and the fee-shifting could encourage suits. The substance was modest and precedent-setting rather than sweeping; notably, a narrower version of the pattern-or-practice provision became law two years later in 1994, which suggests the core idea was workable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its civil-rights subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the Police Accountability Act of 1993 on October 21, 1993.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on November 15, 1993 it went to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights.
No further action was ever taken; the bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and the governments that run them avoided new federal lawsuits, fee awards, a federal excessive-force crime, and mandatory complaint-data reporting.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and sent it to a subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: House members
against.what_they_did: Not a single member signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without a visible coalition to press for action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill was a single-Democrat effort with zero cosponsors from either party, so no party-line split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies and police unions
industries.note: The bill would have exposed departments to federal pattern-or-practice suits, created a federal crime for excessive force, and forced public reporting of complaint data. Its death left departments free of those federal checks.

Governmental bodies would have been liable for winning plaintiffs' attorney fees and would have had to certify data reporting to keep federal justice grants. They bore the direct fiscal cost of the bill's accountability measures.
